claim: Analysis of 458 genomes from individuals residing in the Kalinago Territory of the Commonwealth of Dominica showed approximately 55% Native American, 32% African, and 12% European genetic ancestry.
source: Analysis of 458 genomes from individuals residing in the Kalinago Territory of the Commonwealth of Dominica showed approximately 55% Native American, 32% African, and 12% European genetic ancestry, the highest Native American genetic ancestry among Caribbean populations to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data from 458 individuals and computational analysis using ADMIXTURE and other methods as described in the manuscript.

claim: The Kalinago have the highest Native American genetic ancestry among Caribbean populations to date.
source: Analysis of 458 genomes from individuals residing in the Kalinago Territory of the Commonwealth of Dominica showed approximately 55% Native American, 32% African, and 12% European genetic ancestry, the highest Native American genetic ancestry among Caribbean populations to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the Kalinago genetic ancestry data to published data from other Caribbean populations.

claim: Skin pigmentation in the Kalinago ranged from 20 to 80 melanin units, averaging 46.
source: Skin pigmentation ranged from 20 to 80 melanin units, averaging 46.
evidence: This claim is supported by melanin index measurements from skin reflectometry performed on the sampled individuals.

claim: Three albino individuals were determined to be homozygous for a causative multi-nucleotide polymorphism OCA2NW273KV contained within a haplotype of African origin.
source: Three albino individuals were determined to be homozygous for a causative multi-nucleotide polymorphism OCA2NW273KV contained within a haplotype of African origin; its allele frequency was 0.03 and single allele effect size was –8 melanin units.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole exome sequencing, genotyping data, and local genetic ancestry analysis showing the haplotype is of African origin.

claim: The allele frequency of OCA2NW273KV was 0.03.
source: Three albino individuals were determined to be homozygous for a causative multi-nucleotide polymorphism OCA2NW273KV contained within a haplotype of African origin; its allele frequency was 0.03 and single allele effect size was –8 melanin units.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data from the 458 individuals in the sample.

claim: The single allele effect size of OCA2NW273KV was –8 melanin units.
source: Three albino individuals were determined to be homozygous for a causative multi-nucleotide polymorphism OCA2NW273KV contained within a haplotype of African origin; its allele frequency was 0.03 and single allele effect size was –8 melanin units.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of melanin index data in relation to OCA2NW273KV genotypes.

claim: The derived allele frequency of SLC24A5A111T was 0.14.
source: Derived allele frequencies of SLC24A5A111T and SLC45A2L374F were 0.14 and 0.06, with single allele effect sizes of –6 and –4, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data from the Kalinago sample.

claim: The derived allele frequency of SLC45A2L374F was 0.06.
source: Derived allele frequencies of SLC24A5A111T and SLC45A2L374F were 0.14 and 0.06, with single allele effect sizes of –6 and –4, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data from the Kalinago sample.

claim: The single allele effect size of SLC24A5A111T was –6 melanin units.
source: Derived allele frequencies of SLC24A5A111T and SLC45A2L374F were 0.14 and 0.06, with single allele effect sizes of –6 and –4, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of melanin index data in relation to SLC24A5A111T genotypes.

claim: The single allele effect size of SLC45A2L374F was –4 melanin units.
source: Derived allele frequencies of SLC24A5A111T and SLC45A2L374F were 0.14 and 0.06, with single allele effect sizes of –6 and –4, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of melanin index data in relation to SLC45A2L374F genotypes.

claim: Native American genetic ancestry by itself reduced pigmentation by more than 20 melanin units (range 24–29).
source: Native American genetic ancestry by itself reduced pigmentation by more than 20 melanin units (range 24–29).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of melanin index versus Native American genetic ancestry in individuals lacking the major hypopigmenting alleles.

claim: None of the published polymorphisms predicted in prior literature to affect skin color in Native Americans caused detectable hypopigmentation in the Kalinago.
source: The responsible hypopigmenting genetic variants remain to be identified, since none of the published polymorphisms predicted in prior literature to affect skin color in Native Americans caused detectable hypopigmentation in the Kalinago.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis of previously reported variants showing no significant effects in the Kalinago sample.

claim: Human skin pigmentation is a polygenic trait that is influenced by health and environment.
source: Human skin pigmentation is a polygenic trait that is influenced by health and environment (Barsh, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Lighter skin is most common in populations adapted to northern latitudes characterized by lower UV incidence than equatorial latitudes.
source: Lighter skin is most common in populations adapted to northern latitudes characterized by lower UV incidence than equatorial latitudes (Jablonski and Chaplin, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Selection for lighter skin is biochemically driven by a solar UV-dependent photoactivation step in the formation of vitamin D.
source: Selection for lighter skin, biochemically driven by a solar UV-dependent photoactivation step in the formation of vitamin D (Engelsen, 2010; Hanel and Carlberg, 2020; Holick, 1981; Loomis, 1967) is regarded as the most likely basis for a convergent evolution of lighter skin color in European and East Asian/Native American populations (Lamason et al., 2005; Norton et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on vitamin D synthesis and skin pigmentation evolution.

claim: Convergent evolution of lighter skin color occurred in European and East Asian/Native American populations.
source: Selection for lighter skin, biochemically driven by a solar UV-dependent photoactivation step in the formation of vitamin D (Engelsen, 2010; Hanel and Carlberg, 2020; Holick, 1981; Loomis, 1967) is regarded as the most likely basis for a convergent evolution of lighter skin color in European and East Asian/Native American populations (Lamason et al., 2005; Norton et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on pigmentation evolution.

claim: The A111T allele in SLC24A5 explains at least 25% of the difference in skin color between people of African vs. European genetic ancestry.
source: For example, the A111T allele in SLC24A5 (Lamason et al., 2005) explains at least 25% of the difference in skin color between people of African vs. European genetic ancestry, and is nearly fixed in European populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The A111T allele in SLC24A5 is nearly fixed in European populations.
source: For example, the A111T allele in SLC24A5 (Lamason et al., 2005) explains at least 25% of the difference in skin color between people of African vs. European genetic ancestry, and is nearly fixed in European populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No equivalent polymorphism to SLC24A5A111T in Native Americans or East Asians has been found to date.
source: No equivalent polymorphism in Native Americans or East Asians has been found to date.
evidence: This claim is based on review of prior literature and the absence of such findings.

claim: Native Americans share common genetic ancestry with East Asians.
source: Native Americans share common genetic ancestry with East Asians (Derenko et al., 2010; Tamm et al., 2007), diverging before ~15 kya (Gravel et al., 2013; Moreno-Mayar et al., 2018; Reich et al., 2012), but the extent to which these populations share pigmentation variants remains to be determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on population genetics.

claim: Native Americans and East Asians diverged before ~15 kya.
source: Native Americans share common genetic ancestry with East Asians (Derenko et al., 2010; Tamm et al., 2007), diverging before ~15 kya (Gravel et al., 2013; Moreno-Mayar et al., 2018; Reich et al., 2012), but the extent to which these populations share pigmentation variants remains to be determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on population divergence times.

claim: The derived alleles of rs2333857 and rs6917661 near OPRM1, and rs12668421 and rs11238349 in EGFR are near fixation in some Native American populations.
source: The derived alleles of rs2333857 and rs6917661 near OPRM1, and rs12668421 and rs11238349 in EGFR are near fixation in some Native American populations, but all also have a high frequency in Europeans (Quillen et al., 2012), and none reach genome-wide significance in Adhikari et al., 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on pigmentation genetics.

claim: The derived alleles of rs2333857 and rs6917661 near OPRM1, and rs12668421 and rs11238349 in EGFR all have a high frequency in Europeans.
source: The derived alleles of rs2333857 and rs6917661 near OPRM1, and rs12668421 and rs11238349 in EGFR are near fixation in some Native American populations, but all also have a high frequency in Europeans (Quillen et al., 2012), and none reach genome-wide significance in Adhikari et al., 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: None of rs2333857, rs6917661, rs12668421, and rs11238349 reach genome-wide significance in Adhikari et al., 2019.
source: The derived alleles of rs2333857 and rs6917661 near OPRM1, and rs12668421 and rs11238349 in EGFR are near fixation in some Native American populations, but all also have a high frequency in Europeans (Quillen et al., 2012), and none reach genome-wide significance in Adhikari et al., 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Adhikari et al., 2019 found a significant association for the Y182H variant of MSFD12 with skin color.
source: However, the latter found a significant association for the Y182H variant of MSFD12 with skin color, but its frequencies were only 0.27 and 0.17 in Native Americans and East Asians, respectively, suggesting that it can explain only a small portion of the difference between Native American and/or East Asians and African skin color.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The frequency of the Y182H variant of MSFD12 was 0.27 in Native Americans and 0.17 in East Asians.
source: However, the latter found a significant association for the Y182H variant of MSFD12 with skin color, but its frequencies were only 0.27 and 0.17 in Native Americans and East Asians, respectively, suggesting that it can explain only a small portion of the difference between Native American and/or East Asians and African skin color.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The Y182H variant of MSFD12 can explain only a small portion of the difference between Native American and/or East Asians and African skin color.
source: However, the latter found a significant association for the Y182H variant of MSFD12 with skin color, but its frequencies were only 0.27 and 0.17 in Native Americans and East Asians, respectively, suggesting that it can explain only a small portion of the difference between Native American and/or East Asians and African skin color.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the reported allele frequencies and their expected contribution to pigmentation differences.

claim: Prior to European contact, the Caribbean islands were inhabited by populations who migrated from the northern coast of South America.
source: Prior to European contact, the Caribbean islands were inhabited by populations who migrated from the northern coast of South America (Benn-Torres et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 1969; Honychurch, 2012; Island Caribs, 2016; Benn Torres et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on Caribbean history and population genetics.

claim: During the Colonial period, large numbers of Africans were introduced into the Caribbean as slave labor.
source: During the Colonial period, large numbers of Africans were introduced into the Caribbean as slave labor (Honychurch, 2012; Benn Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical and genetic literature.

claim: Native American genetic ancestry now contributes only a minor portion (<15%) of the genetic ancestry of most Caribbean islanders.
source: As a consequence of African and European admixture and high mortality among the indigenous populations, Native American genetic ancestry now contributes only a minor portion (<15%) of the genetic ancestry of most Caribbean islanders (Auton et al., 2015; Benn Torres et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior genetic studies of Caribbean populations.

claim: The islands of Dominica and St. Vincent were the last colonized by Europeans in the late 1700s.
source: The islands of Dominica and St. Vincent were the last colonized by Europeans in the late 1700s (Honychurch, 2012; Honychurch, 1998; Rogoziński, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: In 1903, the British granted 15 km2 (3700 acres) on the eastern coast of Dominica as a reservation for the Kalinago.
source: In 1903, the British granted 15 km2 (3700 acres) on the eastern coast of Dominica as a reservation for the Kalinago, who were then called 'Carib.'
evidence: This claim is supported by historical documentation cited in the manuscript.

claim: When Dominica gained Independence in 1978, legal rights and a degree of protection from assimilation were gained by the inhabitants of the Carib Reserve.
source: When Dominica gained Independence in 1978, legal rights and a degree of protection from assimilation were gained by the inhabitants of the Carib Reserve (Honychurch, 2012) (redesignated Kalinago Territory in 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical literature.

claim: The Carib Reserve was redesignated Kalinago Territory in 2015.
source: When Dominica gained Independence in 1978, legal rights and a degree of protection from assimilation were gained by the inhabitants of the Carib Reserve (Honychurch, 2012) (redesignated Kalinago Territory in 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical literature.

claim: The Kalinago number about 3000 living within the Territory.
source: Oral history and beliefs among the Kalinago, numbering about 3000 living within the Territory, 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 2 are consistent with the primarily Native American and African genetic ancestry, assessed and confirmed genetically here.
evidence: This claim is based on demographic information about the Kalinago Territory.

claim: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a recessive trait characterized by visual system abnormalities and hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes.
source: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a recessive trait characterized by visual system abnormalities and hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes (Gargiulo et al., 2011; Grønskov et al., 2007; Grønskov et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2006; Vogel et al., 2008) that is caused by mutations in any of a number of autosomal pigmentation genes (Carrasco et al., 2009; Edwards et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2017; Grønskov et al., 2013; Kausar et al., 2013; King et al., 2003; Spritz et al., 1995; Stevens et al., 1997; Stevens et al., 1995; Vogel et al., 2008; Woolf, 2005; Yi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on albinism.

claim: OCA is caused by mutations in any of a number of autosomal pigmentation genes.
source: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a recessive trait characterized by visual system abnormalities and hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes (Gargiulo et al., 2011; Grønskov et al., 2007; Grønskov et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2006; Vogel et al., 2008) that is caused by mutations in any of a number of autosomal pigmentation genes (Carrasco et al., 2009; Edwards et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2017; Grønskov et al., 2013; Kausar et al., 2013; King et al., 2003; Spritz et al., 1995; Stevens et al., 1997; Stevens et al., 1995; Vogel et al., 2008; Woolf, 2005; Yi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on albinism genetics.

claim: The incidence of albinism is ~1:20,000 in populations of European descent.
source: The incidence of albinism is ~1:20,000 in populations of European descent, but much higher in some populations, including many in sub-Saharan Africa (1:5000)(Greaves, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on albinism epidemiology.

claim: The incidence of albinism is much higher in some populations, including many in sub-Saharan Africa (1:5000).
source: The incidence of albinism is ~1:20,000 in populations of European descent, but much higher in some populations, including many in sub-Saharan Africa (1:5000)(Greaves, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on albinism epidemiology.

claim: The DNA and skin color sampling program encompassed 458 individuals, representing 15% of the population of the territory.
source: Our DNA and skin color sampling program encompassed 458 individuals, representing 15% of the population of the territory and all three known albino individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sampling methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: The sampling program included all three known albino individuals in the Kalinago Territory.
source: Our DNA and skin color sampling program encompassed 458 individuals, representing 15% of the population of the territory and all three known albino individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sampling methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: Ages of sampled individuals ranged from 6 to 93.
source: Ages ranged from 6 to 93 (Appendix 1—table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by demographic data collected during sampling.

claim: At K=3, the ADMIXTURE result confirmed three major clusters, corresponding roughly to Africans (black cluster), European/Middle Easterners/Central and South Asians (yellow cluster), and East Asians/Native Americans (green cluster).
source: At K=3, the ADMIXTURE result confirmed the three major clusters, corresponding roughly to Africans (black cluster), European/Middle Easterners/Central and South Asians (yellow cluster), and East Asians/Native Americans (green cluster).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: At K=4, the red component that predominates Native Americans separates the Kalinago from the East Asians (green cluster).
source: At K=4 and higher, the red component that predominates Native Americans separates the Kalinago from the East Asians (green cluster).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: At K=5, a purple cluster (Oceanians) appears.
source: Consistent with prior work (Li et al., 2008), a purple cluster (Oceanians) appears at K=5 and a brown cluster (Central and South Asians) appears at K=6; both are minor sources of genetic ancestry in our Kalinago sample (average <1%) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results and citation to prior work.

claim: At K=6, a brown cluster (Central and South Asians) appears.
source: Consistent with prior work (Li et al., 2008), a purple cluster (Oceanians) appears at K=5 and a brown cluster (Central and South Asians) appears at K=6; both are minor sources of genetic ancestry in our Kalinago sample (average <1%) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results and citation to prior work.

claim: Oceanian and Central and South Asian genetic ancestry are both minor sources of genetic ancestry in the Kalinago sample (average <1%).
source: Consistent with prior work (Li et al., 2008), a purple cluster (Oceanians) appears at K=5 and a brown cluster (Central and South Asians) appears at K=6; both are minor sources of genetic ancestry in our Kalinago sample (average <1%) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results.

claim: At K=4 to K=6, the Kalinago show on average 55% Native American, 32% African, and 11–12% European genetic ancestry.
source: At K=4 to K=6, the Kalinago show on average 55% Native American, 32% African, and 11–12% European genetic ancestry.
evidence: This claim is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results.

claim: The individual with the least admixture has approximately 94% Native American and 6% African genetic ancestry.
source: The individual with the least admixture has approximately 94% Native American and 6% African genetic ancestry.
evidence: This claim is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results.

claim: The Kalinago have more Native American and less European genetic ancestry than any other Caribbean population.
source: Overall, the Kalinago have more Native American and less European genetic ancestry than any other Caribbean population.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of Kalinago genetic ancestry data to published data from other Caribbean populations, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 55% Native American genetic ancestry calculated from autosomal genotype in the Kalinago is greater than the reported 13% in Puerto Rico.
source: The 55% Native American genetic ancestry calculated from autosomal genotype in the Kalinago is greater than the reported 13% in Puerto Rico (Gravel et al., 2013), 10–15% for Tainos across the Caribbean (Schroeder et al., 2018), and 8% for Cubans (Marcheco-Teruel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the Kalinago data to published data from other Caribbean populations.

claim: The 55% Native American genetic ancestry calculated from autosomal genotype in the Kalinago is greater than the reported 10–15% for Tainos across the Caribbean.
source: The 55% Native American genetic ancestry calculated from autosomal genotype in the Kalinago is greater than the reported 13% in Puerto Rico (Gravel et al., 2013), 10–15% for Tainos across the Caribbean (Schroeder et al., 2018), and 8% for Cubans (Marcheco-Teruel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the Kalinago data to published data from other Caribbean populations.

claim: The 55% Native American genetic ancestry calculated from autosomal genotype in the Kalinago is greater than the reported 8% for Cubans.
source: The 55% Native American genetic ancestry calculated from autosomal genotype in the Kalinago is greater than the reported 13% in Puerto Rico (Gravel et al., 2013), 10–15% for Tainos across the Caribbean (Schroeder et al., 2018), and 8% for Cubans (Marcheco-Teruel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the Kalinago data to published data from other Caribbean populations.

claim: The 55% Native American genetic ancestry in the Kalinago is considerably higher than the reported 6% Native American genetic ancestry found in Bwa Mawego, a horticultural population that resides south of the Kalinago Territory.
source: This is also considerably higher than the reported 6% Native American genetic ancestry found in Bwa Mawego, a horticultural population that resides south of the Kalinago Territory (Keith et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the Kalinago data to published data from another population in Dominica.

claim: Crawford et al., 2021 reported 67% Native American genetic ancestry for an independently collected Kalinago sample based on mtDNA haplotype analysis.
source: However, this result is lower than the 67% Native American genetic ancestry reported by Crawford et al., 2021, for an independently collected Kalinago samples based on the mtDNA haplotype analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The difference between 55% autosomal Native American ancestry and 67% mtDNA-based Native American ancestry suggests a paternal bias in combined European and/or African admixture.
source: This difference suggests a paternal bias in combined European and/or African admixture.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of autosomal and mtDNA ancestry estimates.

claim: Samples genotyped using 105 genetic ancestry informative markers from Jamaica and the Lesser Antilles yielded an average of 7.7% Native American genetic ancestry (range 5.6%–16.2%).
source: Samples genotyped using 105 genetic ancestry informative markers from Jamaica and the Lesser Antilles (Benn Torres et al., 2015) yielded an average of 7.7% Native American genetic ancestry (range 5.6%–16.2%), with the highest value from a population in Dominica sampled outside the Kalinago reservation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The highest Native American genetic ancestry value (16.2%) from Benn Torres et al., 2015 was from a population in Dominica sampled outside the Kalinago reservation.
source: Samples genotyped using 105 genetic ancestry informative markers from Jamaica and the Lesser Antilles (Benn Torres et al., 2015) yielded an average of 7.7% Native American genetic ancestry (range 5.6%–16.2%), with the highest value from a population in Dominica sampled outside the Kalinago reservation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The Kalinago population has among the lowest European genetic ancestry (12%) compared to other reported Caribbean Native Americans in St. Kitts (8.2%), Barbados (11.5%), and Puerto Rico (71%).
source: Relevant to the potential mapping of Native American light skin color alleles, the Kalinago population has among the lowest European genetic ancestry (12%) compared to other reported Caribbean Native Americans in St. Kitts (8.2%), Barbados (11.5%), and Puerto Rico (71%) (Benn Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the Kalinago data to published data from other Caribbean populations.

claim: The Kalinago tradition requires that women marrying non-Kalinago leave the Territory.
source: Contributing to the high percentage of Native American genetic ancestry in the Kalinago is their segregation within the 3700 acre Kalinago Territory in Dominica granted by the British in 1903, and the Kalinago tradition that women marrying non-Kalinago are required to leave the Territory; non-Kalinago spouses of Kalinago men are allowed to move to the Territory (KCA, KCC, Personal Communication with Kalinago Council, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on personal communication with the Kalinago Council.

claim: Non-Kalinago spouses of Kalinago men are allowed to move to the Territory.
source: Contributing to the high percentage of Native American genetic ancestry in the Kalinago is their segregation within the 3700 acre Kalinago Territory in Dominica granted by the British in 1903, and the Kalinago tradition that women marrying non-Kalinago are required to leave the Territory; non-Kalinago spouses of Kalinago men are allowed to move to the Territory (KCA, KCC, Personal Communication with Kalinago Council, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on personal communication with the Kalinago Council.

claim: Samples collected outside the Kalinago Territory show lower fractional Native American genetic ancestry.
source: These factors help to explain why samples collected outside the Kalinago Territory (Benn Torres et al., 2013) show lower fractional Native American genetic ancestry.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of genetic ancestry data and knowledge of Kalinago social practices.

claim: Members of the Kalinago community characterized themselves and others in terms of perceived genealogical ancestry as 'Black,' 'Kalinago,' or 'Mixed.'
source: During our fieldwork, it was noted that members of the Kalinago community characterized themselves and others in terms of perceived genealogical ancestry as 'Black,' 'Kalinago,' or 'Mixed.'
evidence: This claim is based on observations during fieldwork.

claim: Individuals self-identified as 'Kalinago' have on average more Native American genetic ancestry (67% vs 51%) than those self-identified as 'Mixed.'
source: Compared to individuals self-identified as 'Mixed,' those self-identified as 'Kalinago' have on average more Native American genetic ancestry (67% vs 51%), less European genetic ancestry (10% vs 14%), and less African genetic ancestry (23% vs 34%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ancestry analysis of individuals grouped by self-identification.

claim: Individuals self-identified as 'Kalinago' have on average less European genetic ancestry (10% vs 14%) than those self-identified as 'Mixed.'
source: Compared to individuals self-identified as 'Mixed,' those self-identified as 'Kalinago' have on average more Native American genetic ancestry (67% vs 51%), less European genetic ancestry (10% vs 14%), and less African genetic ancestry (23% vs 34%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ancestry analysis of individuals grouped by self-identification.

claim: Individuals self-identified as 'Kalinago' have on average less African genetic ancestry (23% vs 34%) than those self-identified as 'Mixed.'
source: Compared to individuals self-identified as 'Mixed,' those self-identified as 'Kalinago' have on average more Native American genetic ancestry (67% vs 51%), less European genetic ancestry (10% vs 14%), and less African genetic ancestry (23% vs 34%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ancestry analysis of individuals grouped by self-identification.

claim: Folk categories based on phenotype are reflected in some underlying differences in genetic ancestry.
source: Thus, these folk categories based on phenotype are reflected in some underlying differences in genetic ancestry.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed correlation between self-identification and genetic ancestry.

claim: Excluding the three albino individuals, the MI in the Kalinago ranged between 28.7 and 79.7 and averaged 45.9.
source: The three Kalinago albino individuals sampled had the lowest values (20.7, 22.4, and 23.8). Excluding these, the MI ranged between 28.7 and 79.7 and averaged 45.9.
evidence: This claim is supported by melanin index measurements from skin reflectometry.

claim: The MI averaged 25 for people of East Asian genetic ancestry as measured with the same equipment in the authors' laboratory.
source: For comparison, the MI averaged 25 and 21 for people of East Asian and European genetic ancestry, respectively, as measured with the same equipment in our laboratory (Ang et al., 2012; Tsetskhladze et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The MI averaged 21 for people of European genetic ancestry as measured with the same equipment in the authors' laboratory.
source: For comparison, the MI averaged 25 and 21 for people of East Asian and European genetic ancestry, respectively, as measured with the same equipment in our laboratory (Ang et al., 2012; Tsetskhladze et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The Kalinago MI range is similar to that of the Senoi of Peninsular Malaysia (MI 24–78; mean = 45.7).
source: This range is similar to that of another indigenous population, the Senoi of Peninsular Malaysia (MI 24–78; mean = 45.7) (Ang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to published data from another population.

claim: The Senoi are believed to include admixture from Malaysian Negritos whose pigmentation is darker (mean = 55).
source: The Senoi are believed to include admixture from Malaysian Negritos whose pigmentation is darker (mean = 55) (Ang et al., 2012) than that of the average Kalinago.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The average MI was 53.4 for Africans in Cape Verde.
source: In comparison, the average MI was 53.4 for Africans in Cape Verde (Beleza et al., 2012) and 59 for African-Americans (Shriver et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The average MI was 59 for African-Americans.
source: In comparison, the average MI was 53.4 for Africans in Cape Verde (Beleza et al., 2012) and 59 for African-Americans (Shriver et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Individuals self-described as 'Kalinago' were slightly lighter and had a narrower MI distribution (42.5± 5.6, mean ± SD) compared to 'Mixed' (45.8± 9.6).
source: Individuals self-described as 'Kalinago' were slightly lighter and had a narrower MI distribution (42.5± 5.6, mean ± SD) compared to 'Mixed' (45.8± 9.6) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by melanin index measurements grouped by self-identification.

claim: The three sampled albino individuals had pale skin (MI 20.7, 22.4, and 23.8 vs. 29–80 for non-albino individuals).
source: The three sampled albino individuals had pale skin (MI 20.7, 22.4, and 23.8 vs. 29–80 for non-albino individuals), showed nystagmus, and reported photophobia and high susceptibility to sunburn.
evidence: This claim is supported by melanin index measurements and clinical observations.

claim: The three sampled albino individuals showed nystagmus.
source: The three sampled albino individuals had pale skin (MI 20.7, 22.4, and 23.8 vs. 29–80 for non-albino individuals), showed nystagmus, and reported photophobia and high susceptibility to sunburn.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical observations.

claim: The three sampled albino individuals reported photophobia and high susceptibility to sunburn.
source: The three sampled albino individuals had pale skin (MI 20.7, 22.4, and 23.8 vs. 29–80 for non-albino individuals), showed nystagmus, and reported photophobia and high susceptibility to sunburn.
evidence: This claim is supported by self-reported symptoms.

claim: The albino individuals had blonde hair and gray irides with varying amounts of green and blue, in contrast to the brown irides and black hair of most Kalinago.
source: In contrast to the brown irides and black hair of most Kalinago, including their parents, the albino individuals had blonde hair and gray irides with varying amounts of green and blue.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic observations.

claim: None of the albino individuals carried any of 28 mutations previously found in African or Native American albino individuals.
source: To identify the albinism variant in the Kalinago, we first determined that none of the albino individuals carried any of 28 mutations previously found in African or Native American albino individuals (Carrasco et al., 2009; King et al., 2003; Stevens et al., 1997; Yi et al., 2003), including a 2.7 kb exon 7 deletion in OCA2 found at high frequency in some African populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping of known albinism mutations.

claim: Whole exome sequencing of one albino individual and one parent revealed 12 variant alleles in 7 OCA genes that were homozygous in the albino individual and heterozygous in the parent.
source: Whole exome sequencing of one albino individual and one parent (obligate carrier) revealed polymorphisms homozygous in the albino individuals and heterozygous in the parent, an initial approach that assumes that the albino individual was not a compound heterozygote. We identified 12 variant alleles in 7 OCA genes (or genomic regions) that met these criteria (summarized in Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole exome sequencing data.

claim: Two missense variants were found in OCA2: SNP rs1800401 (R305W) and multi-nucleotide polymorphism rs797044784 (NW273KV).
source: Two missense variants were found in OCA2: SNP rs1800401 (c.913C>T or p.Arg305Trp in exon 9), R305W, and multi-nucleotide polymorphism rs797044784 in exon 8 (c.819_822delCTGGinsGGTC; p.Asn273_Trp274delinsLysVal), NW273KV.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole exome sequencing data.

claim: Among 458 Kalinago OCA2 genotypes, 26 carried NW273KV and 60 carried R305W.
source: Among 458 Kalinago OCA2 genotypes, 26 carried NW273KV and 60 carried R305W (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data.

claim: Only NW273KV homozygotes were albino individuals.
source: Only NW273KV homozygotes were albino individual.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype-phenotype correlation analysis.

claim: Neither of the two individuals homozygous for R305W but not NW273KV was albino.
source: We know that the allele responsible for albinism was NW273KV because neither of the two individuals, homozygous for R305W but not NW273KV, was albino individual.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype-phenotype correlation analysis.

claim: One individual who was homozygous for R305W and homozygous ancestral for NW273 had an MI of 72, among the darkest in the entire population.
source: In further support of this conclusion is that one individual who was homozygous for R305W and homozygous ancestral for NW273 had an MI of 72, among the darkest in the entire population.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype and phenotype data.

claim: R305W is present with frequency >0.10 in some African, South Asian, and European populations.
source: R305W is notably present with frequency >0.10 in some African, South Asian, and European populations (Auton et al., 2015), predicting a Hardy-Weinberg frequency of homozygotes above 1%.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to population genetic data.

claim: R305W scores incorrectly as pathogenic using SIFT, Polyphen 2.0, and PANTHER.
source: The fact that R305W scores incorrectly as pathogenic using SIFT, Polyphen 2.0, and PANTHER that R305W (Kamaraj and Purohit, 2014) suggests a need for refinement of these methods.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that R305W is not causative for albinism despite being predicted as pathogenic by computational tools.

claim: The universal association of R305W with the NW273KV haplotype indicates that the founder haplotype of the NW273KV albinism mutation carried the silent R305W variant.
source: The universal association of R305W with the NW273KV haplotype indicates that the founder haplotype of the NW273KV albinism mutation carried the silent R305W variant.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from haplotype analysis.

claim: All three albino individuals share a homozygous segment of ~1.7 Mb that encompasses several genes in addition to OCA2.
source: All three albino individuals share a homozygous segment of ~1.7 Mb that encompasses several genes in addition to OCA2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by identity-by-descent analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The albino haplotype defined by homozygosity in individuals 2 and 3 extends ~11 Mb.
source: The albino haplotype defined by homozygosity in individuals 2 and 3 extends ~11 Mb; comparison to local genetic ancestry shows that this haplotype is clearly of African origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by haplotype and local genetic ancestry analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The albino haplotype is clearly of African origin.
source: The albino haplotype defined by homozygosity in individuals 2 and 3 extends ~11 Mb; comparison to local genetic ancestry shows that this haplotype is clearly of African origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by local genetic ancestry analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Kalinago albino individuals are the only reported individuals where the albinism was caused by homozygosity for the NW273KV allele of OCA2.
source: The Kalinago albino individuals are the only reported individuals where the albinism was caused by homozygosity for the NW273KV allele of OCA2.
evidence: This claim is based on review of prior literature and the novel finding in this study.

claim: Two reported albino individuals of African-American/Dutch descent were compound heterozygotes for the OCA2 mutation, with one allele being the NW273KV variant chromosome.
source: Two reported albino individuals of African-American/Dutch descent were compound heterozygotes for the OCA2 mutation, with one allele being the NW273KV variant chromosome (Garrison et al., 2004; Lee et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Conservation of the NW sequence among vertebrates and its inclusion in a potential N-linked glycosylation site supports the variant's pathogenicity.
source: Conservation of the NW sequence among vertebrates and its inclusion in a potential N-linked glycosylation site (Rinchik et al., 1993) that is eliminated by the mutation supports the variant's pathogenicity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence conservation and functional site analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The NW273KV frequency in the Kalinago sample (0.03) translates into a Hardy-Weinberg albinism frequency (p2=0.0009) of ~1 per 1000, as observed (3 in a population of about 3000).
source: The NW273KV frequency in our sample (0.03) translates into a Hardy-Weinberg albinism frequency (p2=0.0009) of ~1 per 1000, as observed (3 in a population of about 3000).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation from allele frequency data and observed albinism frequency.

claim: Examination of publicly available data reveals three OCA2NW273KV heterozygotes in the 1000 Genome Project: a pair of siblings from Barbados (ACB) and one individual from Sierra Leone (MSL).
source: Examination of publicly available data reveals three OCA2NW273KV heterozygotes in the 1000 Genome Project, a pair of siblings from Barbados (ACB) and one individual from Sierra Leone (MSL).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of publicly available genomic data.

claim: The three 1KGP individuals carrying OCA2NW273KV share a haplotype of ~1.5 Mb, of which ~1.0 Mb matches the albino haplotype in the Kalinago.
source: The three 1KGP individuals share a haplotype of ~1.5 Mb, of which ~1.0 Mb matches the albino haplotype in the Kalinago.
evidence: This claim is supported by haplotype analysis of 1000 Genomes Project data.

claim: Each of the variants OCA2NW273KV, SLC24A5A111T, and SLC45A2L374F decreases melanin pigmentation, with homozygotes being lighter than heterozygotes.
source: Each variant decreases melanin pigmentation, with homozygotes being lighter than heterozygotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of melanin index data by genotype shown in Figure 4.

claim: The greatest pigmentation effect is seen in the OCA2NW273KV homozygotes (the albino individuals).
source: The greatest effect is seen in the OCA2NW273KV homozygotes (the albino individuals), as previously noted.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of melanin index data by genotype shown in Figure 4.

claim: The markedly higher frequency of SLC24A5A111T compared to SLC45A2L374F is not explained solely by European admixture.
source: The markedly higher frequency of SLC24A5A111T compared to SLC45A2L374F is not explained solely by European admixture, given that most Europeans are nearly fixed for both alleles (Soejima and Koda, 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from allele frequency data and citation to prior literature.

claim: Most Europeans are nearly fixed for both SLC24A5A111T and SLC45A2L374F alleles.
source: The markedly higher frequency of SLC24A5A111T compared to SLC45A2L374F is not explained solely by European admixture, given that most Europeans are nearly fixed for both alleles (Soejima and Koda, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The Mende of Sierra Leone (MSL) have a SLC24A5A111T frequency of 0.08.
source: Although some sub-Saharan West African populations (the likeliest source of AFR genetic ancestry in the Kalinago) have negligible SLC24A5A111T frequencies, moderate frequencies are found in the Mende of Sierra Leone (MSL, allele frequency = 0.08) (Micheletti et al., 2020; Auton et al., 2015), while some West African populations such as Hausa and Mandinka who have allele frequencies of 0.11 and 0.15, respectively (Cheung et al., 2000; Rajeevan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Hausa and Mandinka populations have SLC24A5A111T allele frequencies of 0.11 and 0.15, respectively.
source: Although some sub-Saharan West African populations (the likeliest source of AFR genetic ancestry in the Kalinago) have negligible SLC24A5A111T frequencies, moderate frequencies are found in the Mende of Sierra Leone (MSL, allele frequency = 0.08) (Micheletti et al., 2020; Auton et al., 2015), while some West African populations such as Hausa and Mandinka who have allele frequencies of 0.11 and 0.15, respectively (Cheung et al., 2000; Rajeevan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The region of chromosome 5 containing SLC45A2 exhibits low European genetic ancestry (6.5%).
source: In addition, the region of chromosome 5 containing SLC45A2 exhibits low European genetic ancestry (6.5%) that is consistent with low observed SLC45A2L374F frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by local genetic ancestry analysis.

claim: One of the three Kalinago albino individuals was heterozygous for SLC24A5A111T, but neither skin nor hair color for this individual was lighter than that of the other two albino individuals.
source: One of the three Kalinago albino individuals was also heterozygous for SLC24A5A111T, but neither skin nor hair color for this individual was lighter than that of the other two albino individuals, who were homozygous for the ancestral allele at SLC24A5A111; this observation is consistent with epistasis of OCA2 hypopigmentation over that of SLC24A5A111T.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes among albino individuals with different SLC24A5 genotypes.

claim: The observation that an albino individual heterozygous for SLC24A5A111T was not lighter than other albino individuals is consistent with epistasis of OCA2 hypopigmentation over that of SLC24A5A111T.
source: One of the three Kalinago albino individuals was also heterozygous for SLC24A5A111T, but neither skin nor hair color for this individual was lighter than that of the other two albino individuals, who were homozygous for the ancestral allele at SLC24A5A111; this observation is consistent with epistasis of OCA2 hypopigmentation over that of SLC24A5A111T.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from phenotypic observations.

claim: The trend toward lighter pigmentation as Native American genetic ancestry increases is clear in individuals lacking the hypopigmenting alleles SLC24A5A111T, SLC45A2L374F, and OCA2NW273KV.
source: The strong dependence of pigmentation on Native American genetic ancestry is clarified by focusing on individuals lacking the hypopigmenting alleles SLC24A5A111T, SLC45A2L374F, and OCA2NW273KV (Figure 5). Although positive deviations from the best fit are apparent at both high and low Native American genetic ancestry, the trend toward lighter pigmentation as Native American genetic ancestry increases is clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The net difference between African and Native American contributions to pigmentation appears likely to be bounded by the magnitudes of the slope vs NAM genetic ancestry (24 units) and the slope vs AFR genetic ancestry (29 units).
source: The net difference between African and Native American contributions to pigmentation appears likely to be bounded by the magnitudes of the slope vs NAM genetic ancestry (24 units) and the slope vs AFR genetic ancestry (29 units, not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of melanin index versus genetic ancestry.

claim: Sex and all three genotyped polymorphisms (SLC24A5A111T, SLC45A2L374F, and OCA2NW273KV) were statistically significant in association analysis.
source: Employing a linear regression model, we found that sex and all three genotyped polymorphisms were statistically significant (Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis results shown in Table 2.

claim: Only SLC24A5A111T reaches genome-wide significance in association analysis.
source: However, only SLC24A5A111T reaches genome-wide significance.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis results.

claim: PC1, which strongly correlated with Native American vs African genetic ancestry, exhibits the lowest p-value in association analysis.
source: PC1, which strongly correlated with Native American vs African genetic ancestry, exhibits the lowest p-value.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis results and principal component analysis.

claim: The effect size for SLC24A5A111T measured in the Kalinago is consistent with previously reported results of –5 melanin units calculated from an African-American sample.
source: The effect size for SLC24A5A111T measured here is consistent with previously reported results of –5 melanin units calculated from an African-American sample (Lamason et al., 2005; Norton et al., 2007) and –5.5 from admixed inhabitants of the Cape Verde islands (Beleza et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current study's results to prior literature.

claim: The effect size for SLC24A5A111T measured in the Kalinago is consistent with –5.5 from admixed inhabitants of the Cape Verde islands.
source: The effect size for SLC24A5A111T measured here is consistent with previously reported results of –5 melanin units calculated from an African-American sample (Lamason et al., 2005; Norton et al., 2007) and –5.5 from admixed inhabitants of the Cape Verde islands (Beleza et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current study's results to prior literature.

claim: Crawford et al., 2017 reported an effect size of –7.7 for SLC24A5A111T in continental Africans.
source: Reported effect sizes for continental Africans are both higher and lower, –7.7 in Crawford et al., 2017, and –3.6 Martin et al., 2017b, while the estimated effect size in the CANDELA study (GWAS of combined admixed populations from Mexico, Brazil, Columbia, Chile, and Peru) (Adhikari et al., 2019) yielded an effect size about –3 melanin units.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Martin et al., 2017b reported an effect size of –3.6 for SLC24A5A111T in continental Africans.
source: Reported effect sizes for continental Africans are both higher and lower, –7.7 in Crawford et al., 2017, and –3.6 Martin et al., 2017b, while the estimated effect size in the CANDELA study (GWAS of combined admixed populations from Mexico, Brazil, Columbia, Chile, and Peru) (Adhikari et al., 2019) yielded an effect size about –3 melanin units.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The CANDELA study yielded an effect size of about –3 melanin units for SLC24A5A111T.
source: Reported effect sizes for continental Africans are both higher and lower, –7.7 in Crawford et al., 2017, and –3.6 Martin et al., 2017b, while the estimated effect size in the CANDELA study (GWAS of combined admixed populations from Mexico, Brazil, Columbia, Chile, and Peru) (Adhikari et al., 2019) yielded an effect size about –3 melanin units.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A significant effect of SLC45A2L374F on skin pigmentation was reported for the African-American sample by Norton et al., 2007.
source: A significant effect of SLC45A2L374F on skin pigmentation reported for the African-American sample by Norton et al., 2007, and in the CANDELA study by Adhikari et al., 2019, but not for the African Caribbean sample by Norton et al., 2007.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A significant effect of SLC45A2L374F on skin pigmentation was reported in the CANDELA study by Adhikari et al., 2019.
source: A significant effect of SLC45A2L374F on skin pigmentation reported for the African-American sample by Norton et al., 2007, and in the CANDELA study by Adhikari et al., 2019, but not for the African Caribbean sample by Norton et al., 2007.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No significant effect of SLC45A2L374F on skin pigmentation was reported for the African Caribbean sample by Norton et al., 2007.
source: A significant effect of SLC45A2L374F on skin pigmentation reported for the African-American sample by Norton et al., 2007, and in the CANDELA study by Adhikari et al., 2019, but not for the African Caribbean sample by Norton et al., 2007.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The 4 unit effect size of SLC45A2L374F in the Kalinago is similar to the 5 unit effect reported by Norton et al., 2007.
source: The 4 unit effect size of this allele in the Kalinago reported here is similar to the 5 unit effect reported by Norton et al., 2007.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current study's results to prior literature.

claim: The estimate that a single OCA2NW273KV allele causes about –8 melanin units of skin lightening is the first reported population-based effect size measurement for any albinism allele.
source: Our estimate that a single OCA2NW273KV allele causes about –8 melanin units of skin lightening is the first reported population-based effect size measurement for any albinism allele.
evidence: This claim is based on the novel finding in this study and review of prior literature.

claim: The albino individuals were lighter by an average of 10 units than predicted from the model.
source: We applied the estimated parameters to the three albino individuals and found that they were lighter by an average of 10 uni nm, 05W homozygotes, when controlling for OCA2NW273KV status, OCA2R305W had no detectable effect on skin color (Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis comparing observed and predicted melanin index values for albino individuals.

claim: When controlling for OCA2NW273KV status, OCA2R305W had no detectable effect on skin color.
source: We applied the estimated parameters to the three albino individuals and found that they were lighter by an average of 10 uni nm, 05W homozygotes, when controlling for OCA2NW273KV status, OCA2R305W had no detectable effect on skin color (Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis controlling for OCA2NW273KV genotype.

claim: Additional Native American hypopigmenting alleles of significant effect size remain to be identified.
source: Additional Native American hypopigmenting alleles of significant effect size remain to be identified.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that known variants do not fully explain the pigmentation differences associated with Native American ancestry.

claim: Previously characterized variants do not explain the pigmentation difference associated with Native American ancestry.
source: Previously characterized variants do not explain this difference.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis of previously reported variants showing no significant effects.

claim: It is possible that multiple hypopigmenting variants of small effect sizes are together required to reach Native American and/or East Asian levels of hypopigmentation.
source: It is possible that multiple hypopigmenting variants of small effect sizes are together required to reach Native American and/or East Asian levels of hypopigmentation, individually having insufficient effect to detect in the Kalinago, given our power limitations.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the inability to identify large-effect variants.

claim: If there are variants with large effect sizes responsible for Native American hypopigmentation, it appears likely that they were not genotyped and are poorly tagged by the genotyped SNPs.
source: Alternatively, if there are variants with large effect sizes, it appears likely that they were not genotyped and are poorly tagged by the genotyped SNPs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the failure to identify such variants in the GWAS.

claim: Melanin index determined from skin reflectance measured at the inner upper arm is commonly used as a measure of constitutive skin pigmentation.
source: MI determined in this way is commonly used as a measure of constitutive skin pigmentation (Choe et al., 2006; Park and Lee, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on skin pigmentation measurement methods.
